result_expr: Derivative(phi(x, y, z, t), t) + M*(6*gamma/eps*phi(x, y, z, t)*(1 - phi(x, y, z, t))*(1 - 2*phi(x, y, z, t)) - 6*gamma*eps*(Derivative(phi(x, y, z, t), (x, 2)) + Derivative(phi(x, y, z, t), (y, 2)) + Derivative(phi(x, y, z, t), (z, 2)))) - alpha*phi(x, y, z, t)**2*(1 - phi(x, y, z, t))**2*(rho_v(x, y, z, t) - rho_vs(T(x, y, z, t)))

symbols.name: M
symbols.meaning: Allen-Cahn interface mobility: how fast the diffuse interface relaxes toward the minimum of F (curvature-driven motion and profile restoration), taken constant

symbols.name: alpha
symbols.meaning: deposition/sublimation kinetic coefficient: rate of change of the ice fraction per unit vapor-density excess at the interface; it absorbs 1/\rho_i and the interface kinetics (sticking coefficient, molecular speed, 1/interface width), taken constant

symbols.name: f
symbols.meaning: bulk double-well density of F, f = 3\gamma/\varepsilon\,\phi^2(1-\phi)^2

symbols.name: mu
symbols.meaning: variational derivative \delta F/\delta\phi (chemical potential of the phase field)

symbols.name: g
symbols.meaning: interface indicator weighting the source, g = \phi^2(1-\phi)^2

symbols.name: phi0
symbols.meaning: equilibrium flat-interface profile along the normal coordinate X

symbols.name: X
symbols.meaning: coordinate normal to a flat interface

steps.title: Derivative of the double well
steps.why: The variational derivative of $F$ needs $f'(\phi)$ for the bulk part of the integrand.

steps.title: Variational derivative of F
steps.why: Vary $\phi$ in $F$, integrate the gradient term by parts (boundary term dropped for no-flux or periodic boundaries) to get the Euler-Lagrange derivative $\mu$.
steps.operation: first variation and integration by parts

steps.title: Equilibrium profile and no-nucleation weight
steps.why: The flat profile $\phi_0=\tfrac12[1+\tanh(X/2\varepsilon)]$ makes $\mu=0$, so relaxation keeps the given interface structure. The phase-change source must vanish in pure ice and pure gas (no nucleation, A4), so it is weighted by $g(\phi)=\phi^2(1-\phi)^2$, which vanishes with zero slope at $\phi=0,1$.
steps.operation: substitution of the tanh profile; evaluation of $g$ and $g'$ at 0 and 1

check.printed: S3 deltaF/deltaphi on tanh profile = 0; g(0), g(1), g'(0), g'(1) = [0, 0, 0, 0]

steps.title: Evolution law
steps.why: The non-conserved phase field relaxes down the gradient of $F$ (Allen-Cahn, A3) and is driven by the supersaturation $\rho_v-\rho_{vs}(T)$ at the interface (A5). Positive supersaturation gives $\partial_t\phi>0$ (deposition); with the source off, $dF/dt=-M\int\mu^2\,dV\le 0$.
steps.operation: add the gradient-flow term and the weighted source

check.printed: S4 source sign at phi=1/2, rho_v-rho_vs=+1: 1

steps.title: Residual in 3D Cartesian form
steps.why: Substitute $\mu$ from S2 and $g$ from S3 into S4 and move everything to one side. Every term has units of s$^{-1}$.
steps.operation: substitution of S2 and S3 into S4

assumptions_used: A1: $\rho_v$ and $T$ are known, smooth fields (given).
A2: $F$ gives a flat interface with energy $\gamma$ per area and 10-90% width $2\ln 9\,\varepsilon$ (given).

A3: $\phi$ is a non-conserved order parameter. Near coexistence it follows a linear gradient flow (Allen-Cahn) with a constant mobility $M$; boundaries are no-flux or periodic, so the boundary term from the integration by parts drops out.
A4: There is no nucleation, so the phase-change source vanishes where $\phi=0$ or $\phi=1$. It is localized at the interface by $g(\phi)=\phi^2(1-\phi)^2$; this specific shape is a modeling choice.
A5: The growth rate is linear in the supersaturation $\rho_v-\rho_{vs}(T)$, with a constant kinetic coefficient $\alpha$ that absorbs $1/\rho_i$ and the attachment kinetics.
A6: The ice is rigid and at rest; there is no advection of $\phi$.

neglected.why: The relaxation term $-M\mu$ already produces curvature-driven motion. The explicit shift $\rho_{vs}\,2\gamma v_m/(\kappa_B T r)$ is about $10^{-2}$ for $r\sim 0.1\,\mu$m and smaller for larger pores.
Kept constant for simplicity. They can be promoted to $M(\phi,T)$ and $\alpha(\phi,T)$ without changing the structure of the equation.

neglected.effect: Anisotropy of $\gamma$ and of the attachment kinetics (facets)
neglected.why: Ice basal and prismatic surface energies differ by only a few percent. The model is isotropic.
Grains are not part of this two-phase model; they would enter as boundary conditions or a third phase.

neglected.effect: Density change, mechanical stress and flow of ice
neglected.why: Ice is rigid at about 200 K on the time scales of interest. Stress energy is small compared with $\gamma/\varepsilon$.
$\kappa_B T$ is much smaller than $\gamma\varepsilon^2$ for $\varepsilon$ above about 1 nm, so fluctuations are negligible.

neglected.effect: Coupling of the source to the vapor and heat equations (mass sink, latent heat)
neglected.why: Not neglected physically. It belongs to the separate $\rho_v$ and $T$ tasks, since here $\rho_v$ and $T$ are given fields.

questions: The interface weight $g(\phi)=\phi^2(1-\phi)^2$ and the constant $M$, $\alpha$ are my modeling choices (as in Moure & Fu-type ice models). If the reference model uses another weight, such as $\phi(1-\phi)$ or $30\phi^2(1-\phi)^2$, or a source divided explicitly by $\rho_i$, the coefficient $\alpha$ changes accordingly.
